questions.question: Define urbanisation, migration and related terms, and describe urbanisation in Africa and South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: Urbanisation is the increase in the proportion of a country's population living in urban areas; it differs from city growth, which can happen without the urban share rising. Cities grow by natural increase and by migration, the movement of people to live elsewhere; rural-urban migration is the main cause of urbanisation in Africa. Migration may be internal, such as from the Eastern Cape to Gauteng, or international, such as from Zimbabwe to South Africa, and voluntary or forced; refugees flee war or persecution. More than half of the world's people are urban; Africa has roughly two in five people in urban areas but is urbanising fastest, with cities such as Lagos, Kinshasa, Cairo, Luanda, Nairobi and Dar es Salaam growing enormously. South Africa is about two-thirds urban, and Gauteng, about 1.5 per cent of the land, had about 15.1 million of 62.0 million people in 2022, about 24 per cent.

questions.question: Explain the push factors that drive people out of rural areas in South Africa and Africa.
questions.expected_answer: Economic push factors are the strongest: few jobs outside seasonal, poorly paid farm work and high unemployment, especially in former homeland areas of the Eastern Cape, Limpopo and KwaZulu-Natal. Farming problems include small, overcrowded and overused plots, soil erosion, lack of money for inputs, droughts and floods, and climate change, while land dispossession through the 1913 Land Act and the homelands left many families with too little land. Lack of services includes poorly resourced schools, few clinics, long distances, poor roads and in places no piped water or electricity, and few colleges. Social and political factors include conflict, violence, crime, discrimination and family problems, with wars in places such as the DRC, Somalia, South Sudan and Sudan forcing millions to flee. Natural disasters such as Cyclone Idai in 2019 displaced hundreds of thousands. Push factors usually act together.

questions.question: Explain the pull factors of cities and how households decide whether to migrate.
questions.expected_answer: Cities pull people with the hope of employment and higher incomes in factories, shops, offices, construction, transport, domestic work and the informal sector; with better services such as schools, colleges, universities, clinics, hospitals, water, electricity, sanitation, shops and banks; and with social attractions, especially family and friends who help newcomers find housing and work, called chain migration, as well as entertainment and freedom. Some pull factors are perceptions, and migrants may find unemployment, costly transport, crowded housing and crime, but often stay because opportunities are still better. Decisions are often made by households, which send a young adult to earn money and send remittances home, a major income in rural areas, and migrants keep links with rural homes. People weigh push factors, pull factors and obstacles such as cost, distance, border controls and lack of information.
